modules.title: Persuasion and debate
modules.summary: Argue under pressure: emphasise with inversion, hedge with precision and rebut without hostility.

grammar.name: Inversion for emphasis: Not only…, Rarely…
grammar.explanation: After a negative or limiting adverbial at the start of a sentence, invert the subject and auxiliary to add emphasis.
keyPoints: Not only did the policy cut emissions, but it also created jobs.
Rarely have I seen such a weak argument.
Never before has the city faced this choice. / Little did we know…
grammar.example: Not only did the levy reduce consumption, but it also funded school meals; rarely has a policy faced such organised opposition.

items.prompt: Not only ___ the policy cut emissions, but it also created jobs.
items.explanation: Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb: Not only did the policy cut emissions…
A fronted negative adverbial triggers inversion: Rarely have I heard…

options: Never the city has faced this choice.
Never has the city faced this choice.
Never has faced the city this choice.
items.answer: Never has the city faced this choice.
items.explanation: Auxiliary before subject, then the main verb.

grammar.name: Hedging: It appears that…, This may suggest…
grammar.explanation: Hedging shows how confident you are, protects you from overclaiming and makes debate sound reasonable rather than dogmatic.
keyPoints: It appears that the data supports the claim, although further study is needed.
This may suggest a link between the two, rather than prove one.
Use tend to, arguably, to some extent and it is likely that to soften claims.
grammar.example: The figures appear to support the tax, although they may also reflect a broader change in buying habits.

items.prompt: Which sentence is best hedged for an academic essay?
options: The evidence suggests that sugar taxes tend to reduce consumption.
items.answer: The evidence suggests that sugar taxes tend to reduce consumption.
items.explanation: Suggests and tend to signal limited confidence without weakening the point.

items.prompt: This ___ suggest a link, but it does not prove one.
items.explanation: May expresses possibility and keeps the claim proportionate.
Beyond doubt is an absolute claim, the opposite of hedging.

vocab.example: Her closing argument was quietly persuasive.

vocab.example: I concede the point about cost, but not about fairness.

vocab.definition: a suggested plan of action for an organisation

vocab.definition: shared opinions or interests

vocab.example: She rebutted the claim in two sentences.

inputs.title: Panel debate: should cities ban cars from the centre?
inputs.body: HOST: Is a car-free centre realistic? COUNCILLOR REID: Not only has it worked elsewhere, but it has also increased footfall in the shops. That is the part people miss. TRADER MS KOVAC: With respect, that has not been our experience. Our deliveries arrive before seven, and the loading bay is gone. COUNCILLOR REID: Then let us concede that point and solve it — timed access. MS KOVAC: I would accept timed access, provided it is enforced. My worry is that it looks good in a report and fails in the street.

questions.prompt: What does Councillor Reid claim about shops?
What does Ms Kovac accept in the end?

inputs.title: How to write a proposal that gets read
inputs.body: Most proposals fail for a boring reason: the reader cannot find the recommendation. A useful proposal opens with the decision required, not with background. It states the problem in one paragraph, the options in three, and the recommendation in one sentence that could be quoted. Evidence should be proportionate: two strong figures persuade more than ten weak ones. Finally, anticipate the objection your reader will raise and answer it on the page, in their words. Not only does this show respect, but it also removes the easiest reason to say no.

questions.prompt: What should a proposal open with?
What does the writer advise about evidence?

speaking.title: Three-minute persuasive monologue and rebuttal
speaking.prompt: Choose a policy you would change. Present it in two minutes, then respond to a counter-argument read aloud in the third minute.
phrases: Not only does this..., but it also...

speaking.title: Role-play: negotiating with an opponent
speaking.prompt: You are negotiating a joint statement with someone who opposes your position. Find common ground, concede one point and secure one commitment. Two to three minutes.
phrases: What would you need in return?

speaking.title: Shadowing: inversion under pressure
speaking.prompt: Shadow the clip, keeping the falling intonation on the inverted clause and the pause before the rebuttal.
phrases: Not only did the policy work, / but it also / won over its critics.

writing.title: Formal proposal: a change worth making
writing.prompt: Write a 180–200-word formal proposal to a decision-maker recommending one change to a policy you know. Include the decision required, the options and a clear recommendation.

outline.analyze: Purpose: secure a decision. Audience: a busy official. Register: formal and direct.
outline.plan: Decision required → problem → three options → recommendation → one anticipated objection.
outline.draft: Use one inversion, two hedges and a conditional offer (provided that).
outline.improve: Cut background; make the recommendation quotable in one sentence.
outline.review: Check that a reader could act on the proposal after one reading.

lessons.title: Inversion for emphasis
lessons.objective: Front a negative adverbial and invert the subject and auxiliary correctly.
lessons.canDo: I can add emphasis with Not only, Rarely and Little did without breaking word order.
lessons.output: Record five sentences using inversion to emphasise a real opinion.

lessons.title: Hedging: saying it without overclaiming
lessons.objective: Calibrate certainty with it appears that, may suggest and tend to.
lessons.canDo: I can express confidence at the right level instead of overclaiming.
lessons.output: Take five strong claims and rewrite each one with appropriate hedging.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: persuasion and evidence
lessons.objective: Debate with ten precise expressions for arguments, evidence and concessions.
lessons.canDo: I can name the parts of an argument and evaluate evidence precisely.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds evaluating an argument you have heard recently.

lessons.title: Listening: should cities ban cars?
lessons.objective: Track positions, concessions and conditions across a heated panel.
lessons.canDo: I can follow a panel debate and note who conceded what and on which condition.
lessons.output: Note each speaker's position, one concession and one condition.

lessons.title: Reading: writing a proposal that gets read
lessons.objective: Extract the recommended structure and the writer's advice on evidence.
lessons.canDo: I can read advice on formal writing and apply its structure to my own proposal.
lessons.output: Turn the article into a five-point checklist for your own proposal.

lessons.title: Speaking: persuade, then rebut
lessons.objective: Deliver a three-minute persuasive case and answer a counter-argument.
lessons.canDo: I can present a persuasive case and rebut an objection without losing composure.
lessons.output: Use the prompt card: two minutes of argument, one minute of rebuttal.

lessons.title: Writing: formal proposal
lessons.objective: Write a decision-ready proposal of 180–200 words.
lessons.canDo: I can write a formal proposal with a clear recommendation and an anticipated objection.
lessons.output: Draft, then cut every sentence that does not serve the decision.

lessons.title: Review: timed interactive discussion
lessons.objective: Sustain a ten-minute discussion with a partner, using the module's tools under pressure.
lessons.canDo: I can hold my own in a ten-minute discussion, hedging, conceding and rebutting appropriately.
lessons.output: Record a ten-minute simulation: present, respond, concede and conclude.

modules.title: B2 consolidation
modules.summary: Pull it together: mixed-skill practice under time pressure, then the final B2 assessment.
modules.vocabularyTopic: High-value B2 lexis for argument and evaluation

grammar.name: Review: perfect and narrative aspects
grammar.explanation: B2 accuracy in the perfect family comes from choosing by meaning: present perfect for relevance now, past perfect for a prior past point, and perfect continuous for duration.
keyPoints: Relevance now: I have been working on this since March.
Prior past: By the time the study was published, the policy had already changed.
Duration before a past point: They had been negotiating for months.
grammar.example: I have been studying for two years, and by the time I finish, I will have completed eleven courses.

items.explanation: Since + a point in time with an ongoing activity requires the present perfect continuous.

items.prompt: By the time the study was published, the policy ___.
items.explanation: The change happened before a past publication, so the past perfect is required.

items.prompt: They ___ for months before the agreement was signed.
items.explanation: Duration before a past event takes the past perfect continuous.

grammar.name: Review: conditionals, modals and reported speech
grammar.explanation: At B2 these systems are combined: conditionals carry modal meaning, modality shifts in reported speech, and hedging keeps claims proportionate.
keyPoints: Had they consulted residents, the plan would have passed.
She said it might have been avoided if the notice had been longer.
It may be that the figures understate the effect.
grammar.example: Had the consultation been longer, the council might not have lost the vote; several members said they would have supported a revised plan.

items.prompt: ___ they consulted residents, the plan would have passed.
items.explanation: Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle.

items.prompt: She said it ___ if the notice had been longer.
items.explanation: Reported past possibility with a passive: might have been avoided.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most cautious?
options: The figures may understate the effect.
The figures definitely understate the effect.
items.answer: The figures may understate the effect.
items.explanation: May keeps the claim provisional, which is the safest B2 academic choice.

vocab.example: The benefits outweigh the costs in the long run.

vocab.definition: certain to happen and impossible to avoid
vocab.example: Some disruption is inevitable during the works.

vocab.definition: reduce the harmful effects of something
vocab.example: Trees mitigate the heat in dense districts.

vocab.definition: common in a particular place or time

vocab.definition: causing harm

vocab.definition: possible and practical to do
vocab.example: A partial ban is feasible within a year.

inputs.title: Timed listening: three accents, one topic
inputs.body: SPEAKER 1: I grew up in a city where nobody cycled, and now there are more bikes than cars on my old street. SPEAKER 2: The infrastructure came first, which is the opposite of what most cities try. You cannot ask people to change and then blame them when there is nowhere safe to go. SPEAKER 3: What interests me is the budget. Cycle lanes are cheap compared with a motorway, yet they are treated as a luxury. If the same money had gone into roads, nobody would have questioned it.

questions.prompt: What does Speaker 2 say cities usually do wrong?
options: Build infrastructure after asking people to change
questions.answer: Build infrastructure after asking people to change

options: Cycle lanes are treated as a luxury
questions.answer: Cycle lanes are treated as a luxury

inputs.title: Timed reading: the limits of a good statistic
inputs.body: A single impressive number can end a discussion before it starts, which is precisely why it deserves suspicion. Take the claim that a policy 'created ten thousand jobs'. The figure may be accurate and still misleading: it says nothing about whether those jobs replaced others, how long they lasted, or who got them. Serious evaluation asks for the counterfactual — what would have happened anyway — and that is the question a headline rarely answers. Readers who learn to ask it become considerably harder to persuade with a number alone.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer distrust impressive numbers?
options: They can be accurate yet misleading
questions.answer: They can be accurate yet misleading

questions.prompt: What question does serious evaluation ask?

speaking.title: Final speaking: three-minute opinion talk
speaking.prompt: Some people believe remote work improves productivity. Do you agree? Give reasons and examples. Speak for three minutes using at least three linking expressions and two topic-specific terms.
phrases: A good illustration of this is...

speaking.title: Speaking interview: follow-up questions
speaking.prompt: Answer three follow-up questions on your talk: one asking for evidence, one challenging your position, one asking for a prediction.
phrases: I would qualify that by saying...

speaking.title: Shadowing: B2 prosody capstone
speaking.prompt: Shadow the model twice: stress the contrast, chunk the thought groups and keep the intonation falling on statements.
phrases: What matters / is not how fast you speak, / but how clearly / you are understood.

writing.title: Final essay: an argument with examples
writing.prompt: Write a 200–220-word argument essay: is remote work better for productivity and wellbeing? Present both sides, use evidence, and reach a clear conclusion.

outline.analyze: Purpose: argue and conclude. Audience: an examiner. Register: formal.
outline.plan: Introduction with position → for → against → evaluation → conclusion.
outline.draft: Use one inversion, two hedges, two advanced linkers and one conditional.
outline.improve: Replace generic claims with qualified ones; add one concrete example.
outline.review: Check the essay answers the question, not merely the topic.

lessons.title: Review: perfect and narrative aspects
lessons.objective: Choose accurately across the perfect family in extended speech.
lessons.canDo: I can use perfect and narrative aspects accurately when I speak at length.
lessons.output: Record 90 seconds on your last two years using four perfect forms.

lessons.title: Review: conditionals, modals and reported speech
lessons.objective: Combine conditionals, modality and reported speech without losing accuracy.
lessons.canDo: I can combine conditionals and reported speech accurately in a complex sentence.
lessons.output: Write and record five complex sentences joining a conditional to reported speech.

lessons.title: Review: modals of deduction and hedging
lessons.objective: Calibrate certainty across a long answer.
lessons.canDo: I can express certainty, possibility and doubt precisely across a long turn.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds speculating about a news story with graded certainty.

lessons.title: Vocabulary consolidation: B2 lexis
lessons.objective: Recall and use ten high-value B2 items in argument.
lessons.canDo: I can use precise B2 academic lexis to evaluate an argument.
lessons.output: Record 90 seconds using eight of the ten items naturally.

lessons.title: Timed listening: three accents
lessons.objective: Hold comprehension across accents and note-taking under time pressure.
lessons.canDo: I can follow three accents on one topic and take usable notes without a transcript.
lessons.output: Take notes while listening once, then summarise in four sentences.

lessons.objective: Answer inference questions in a fixed time without rereading everything.
lessons.canDo: I can answer inference questions against the clock with a defensible reason.

lessons.title: Writing: final essay
lessons.objective: Produce a 200–220-word essay under exam conditions.
lessons.canDo: I can write a timed 200–220-word argument essay with evidence and a conclusion.
lessons.output: Write in 30 minutes, then spend five minutes editing for linkers and hedging.

lessons.title: Speaking: final B2 capstone
lessons.objective: Sustain a three-minute talk plus follow-up questions.
lessons.canDo: I can speak for three minutes on an abstract question and handle follow-ups confidently.
lessons.output: Use the final prompt card, then answer the three follow-up questions.
